CausalChain: Chronic biliary inflammation and bile stasis -> Activation of CAFs in the tumor microenvironment -> Secretion of exosomes enriched with non-coding RNAs -> Uptake by cholangiocytes -> Epigenetic reprogramming of gene expression -> Induction of EMT and acquisition of stem-like properties -> Enhanced chemoresistance and tumor progression
Hypothesis: CAF-derived exosomes carrying specific non-coding RNAs induce epigenetic changes in cholangiocytes, driving EMT and stemness acquisition that promote chemoresistance and tumor heterogeneity in cholangiocarcinoma.
Abstract: Recent insights into cholangiocarcinoma underscore a multifaceted interplay between the tumor microenvironment, epigenetic deregulation, and non-coding RNA dynamics. Emerging data suggest that cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) contribute to a protumorigenic milieu through paracrine communication. We propose that CAF-derived exosomes, enriched in specific non-coding RNAs, can deliver epigenetic modulators to cholangiocytes. This horizontal transfer leads to reprogramming of gene expression, promoting epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), acquisition of cancer stem cell traits, and ultimately, chemoresistance. This hypothesis integrates chronic inflammatory signaling, CAF activation, non-coding RNA-mediated epigenetic modulation, and resultant tumor heterogeneity, offering a novel avenue for targeted interventions in cholangiocarcinoma.
